entity<|#|>Egyptian Civil Code<|#|>Content<|#|>The Egyptian Civil Code (القانون المدني المصري) is a comprehensive legislative document governing civil matters in Egypt, including laws, rights, legal capacity, conflicts of law, and various civil obligations.
entity<|#|>National Courts<|#|>Organization<|#|>National Courts (المحاكم الوطنية) are Egyptian judicial bodies that previously operated under an older civil law issued on October 28, 1883.
entity<|#|>Mixed Courts<|#|>Organization<|#|>Mixed Courts (المحاكم المختلطة) are Egyptian judicial bodies that previously operated under an older civil law issued on June 28, 1875.
entity<|#|>Minister of Justice<|#|>Person<|#|>The Minister of Justice (وزير العدل) is the official responsible for executing and implementing the Egyptian Civil Code, which came into force on October 15, 1949.
entity<|#|>Qasr El-Qubba<|#|>Location<|#|>Qasr El-Qubba (قصر القبة) is the palace in Cairo where the Egyptian Civil Code was issued on July 16, 1948 (9 Ramadan 1367).
entity<|#|>Custom<|#|>Concept<|#|>Custom (العرف) is a source of law applied by judges when no legislative provision exists, serving as a secondary legal reference after statutory law.
entity<|#|>Islamic Sharia<|#|>Concept<|#|>Islamic Sharia (الشريعة الإسلامية) is a source of law applied by judges in the absence of both legislative provisions and custom, serving as a tertiary legal reference in the Egyptian Civil Code.
entity<|#|>Natural Justice<|#|>Concept<|#|>Natural Justice (القانون الطبيعي) is a legal principle applied by judges as a final source of law when no legislative provision, custom, or Islamic Sharia principle is available.
entity<|#|>Rules of Equity<|#|>Concept<|#|>The Rules of Equity (قواعد العدالة) are legal principles applied alongside natural justice when no other legal source is available.
entity<|#|>Legal Capacity<|#|>Concept<|#|>Legal Capacity (الأهلية) refers to the legal competence of persons as defined by legislative provisions, applicable to all persons fulfilling the conditions embodied in such provisions.
entity<|#|>Prescription<|#|>Concept<|#|>Prescription (التقادم) refers to legal time limits, with new legislative provisions applying from the time they come into force for incomplete prescription periods.
entity<|#|>Gregorian Calendar<|#|>Concept<|#|>The Gregorian Calendar (التقويم الميلادي) is the standard calendar used for calculating periods of limitation under the Egyptian Civil Code unless otherwise specified.
entity<|#|>Egypt<|#|>Location<|#|>Egypt is the sovereign state whose law serves as the primary reference for characterizing legal relationships in conflicts of law and governs various civil matters within its territory.
entity<|#|>Marriage<|#|>Concept<|#|>Marriage (الزواج) is a legal institution whose validity conditions are governed by the national law of each spouse, and its effects are regulated by the law of the husband's country at the time of conclusion.
entity<|#|>Inheritance<|#|>Concept<|#|>Inheritance (الميراث) and wills are governed by the national law of the deceased, testator, or person disposing of property at the time of death.
entity<|#|>Contractual Obligations<|#|>Concept<|#|>Contractual Obligations (الالتزامات التعاقدية) are governed by the law of the common domicile of the contracting parties, or by the law of the place where the contract was concluded.
entity<|#|>Non-Contractual Obligations<|#|>Concept<|#|>Non-Contractual Obligations (الالتزامات غير التعاقدية) are governed by the law of the state in whose territory the act giving rise to the obligation took place.
entity<|#|>Private International Law<|#|>Concept<|#|>Private International Law (القانون الدولي الخاص) applies in cases of conflict of laws for which no specific provision is made in the Egyptian Civil Code.
entity<|#|>Judge<|#|>Person<|#|>The Judge (القاضي) is the judicial authority responsible for deciding cases using various sources of law and determining applicable law in cases involving persons of unknown or plural nationality.
relation<|#|>Egyptian Civil Code<|#|>National Courts<|#|>repeal, replacement<|#|>The Egyptian Civil Code repealed the previous civil law applied before National Courts and replaced it with a new comprehensive civil code.
relation<|#|>Egyptian Civil Code<|#|>Mixed Courts<|#|>repeal, replacement<|#|>The Egyptian Civil Code repealed the previous civil law applied before Mixed Courts and replaced it with a new comprehensive civil code.
relation<|#|>Minister of Justice<|#|>Egyptian Civil Code<|#|>execution, implementation<|#|>The Minister of Justice is tasked with executing and implementing the Egyptian Civil Code starting from October 15, 1949.
relation<|#|>Egyptian Civil Code<|#|>Qasr El-Qubba<|#|>issuance location<|#|>The Egyptian Civil Code was issued at Qasr El-Qubba on July 16, 1948.
relation<|#|>Judge<|#|>Custom<|#|>legal hierarchy, judicial decision-making<|#|>The Judge applies custom as a source of law when no applicable legislative provision exists.
relation<|#|>Judge<|#|>Islamic Sharia<|#|>legal hierarchy, judicial decision-making<|#|>The Judge applies principles of Islamic Sharia when neither legislative provisions nor custom are available.
relation<|#|>Judge<|#|>Natural Justice<|#|>legal hierarchy, judicial decision-making<|#|>The Judge applies principles of natural justice when legislative provisions, custom, and Islamic Sharia principles are all absent.
relation<|#|>Legal Capacity<|#|>Egypt<|#|>legal governance, personal status<|#|>Legal capacity provisions apply to all persons who fulfill the conditions set by Egyptian legislative provisions.
relation<|#|>Prescription<|#|>Gregorian Calendar<|#|>time calculation, legal period<|#|>Prescription periods are calculated according to the Gregorian Calendar unless expressly provided otherwise by law.
relation<|#|>Marriage<|#|>Egypt<|#|>legal governance, territorial application<|#|>If one spouse is Egyptian at the time of marriage, Egyptian law alone applies to the marriage's conditions and effects.
relation<|#|>Inheritance<|#|>Egypt<|#|>legal governance, succession law<|#|>Inheritance and wills are governed by the national law of the deceased or testator at the time of death, with Egyptian law applying in certain circumstances.
relation<|#|>Contractual Obligations<|#|>Egypt<|#|>legal governance, choice of law<|#|>Contractual obligations are governed by the law of the common domicile of contracting parties or the law of the place of contract conclusion, with Egyptian law applying for immovable contracts in Egypt.
relation<|#|>Non-Contractual Obligations<|#|>Egypt<|#|>legal governance, tort law<|#|>Non-contractual obligations arising from torts are governed by the law of the place where the act occurred, with Egyptian law applying exceptions for acts lawful in Egypt but unlawful abroad.
relation<|#|>Private International Law<|#|>Egyptian Civil Code<|#|>supplementary law, conflict resolution<|#|>Private International Law principles apply as a supplementary framework for conflicts of law not specifically addressed in the Egyptian Civil Code.
relation<|#|>Judge<|#|>Egypt<|#|>judicial authority, legal determination<|#|>The Judge determines the applicable law for persons of unknown or plural nationality, with Egyptian law applying when a person holds Egyptian nationality alongside foreign nationalities.

entity<|#|>Stipulator<|#|>Person<|#|>A party who makes a stipulation in favor of a third party in a contract; may revoke the stipulation before the beneficiary claims it, substitute a new beneficiary, or retain the benefit for himself.
entity<|#|>Beneficiary<|#|>Person<|#|>A third party in whose favor a stipulation is made; may be a future person or institution not yet identified at the date of the contract, provided identification is possible when the contract takes effect.
entity<|#|>Debtor<|#|>Person<|#|>A party obligated under a contract; revocation of a third-party stipulation does not liberate the debtor vis-a-vis the stipulator unless expressly agreed.

entity<|#|>Damages<|#|>Concept<|#|>Compensation for injury or loss awarded by a judge; may consist of a money payment paid in installments, a regular periodical payment, restoration of the original position, or performance of a specific act connected to the unlawful act.

entity<|#|>Reward<|#|>Concept<|#|>A prize promised to the public in exchange for a specified service; the promisor is bound to pay whoever performs the service, even without knowledge of the promise, and may withdraw the promise by public notice.
entity<|#|>Unlawful Act<|#|>Concept<|#|>A fault causing injury to another that imposes an obligation of reparation on the person who committed it; forms the basis for tort liability and may give rise to a damages action prescribed after three years.
entity<|#|>Force Majeure<|#|>Concept<|#|>Unforeseeable circumstances or irresistible force beyond a person's control that exempt liability for injury, alongside unforeseen circumstances, the fault of the victim, or the fault of a third party.
entity<|#|>Legitimate Defense<|#|>Concept<|#|>Self-defense of one's own person or property, or that of a third party; exempts a person from liability for causing injury, provided the defensive measures do not exceed what is necessary.
entity<|#|>Public Official<|#|>Person<|#|>A government employee who is not liable for causing injury if acting in pursuance of a superior's order that he was obliged to obey, provided he had reasonable grounds to believe the act was lawful and acted with care.
entity<|#|>Victim<|#|>Person<|#|>A person who suffers injury from an unlawful act and may claim damages; the right of action is prescribed after three years from knowledge of the injury and the responsible person, or fifteen years from the unlawful act.

entity<|#|>Master<|#|>Person<|#|>A person who has actual powers of supervision and control over a servant; liable for damage caused by the servant's unlawful acts performed in the course of or as a result of employment.
entity<|#|>Servant<|#|>Person<|#|>A person under the employment and control of a master; the master-servant relationship exists when the master has actual powers of supervision and direction over the servant.
entity<|#|>Animal Keeper<|#|>Person<|#|>A person in charge of an animal, even if not its owner, who is liable for harm caused by the animal even if it strays or escapes, unless the harm resulted from a cause beyond the keeper's control.
entity<|#|>Animal<|#|>Creature<|#|>A living creature under the care of an animal keeper; harm caused by the animal gives rise to the keeper's strict liability.
entity<|#|>Building Keeper<|#|>Person<|#|>A person in charge of a building, even if not its owner, who is liable for damage caused by the building's collapse.
entity<|#|>Penal Offence<|#|>Concept<|#|>A criminal offense from which a damages claim may arise; when the penal action has not yet prescribed, the civil damages action is only prescribed when the penal action itself is prescribed.

entity<|#|>Article 310<|#|>Content<|#|>A legal provision stating that when an assignee exercises the right of recourse in warranty against the assignor in accordance with the two preceding articles, the assignor is only liable to restitute what he has received together with interest and expenses notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary.
entity<|#|>Article 311<|#|>Content<|#|>A legal provision stating that an assignor is responsible for personal acts, even if the assignment is not for valuable consideration or even if it has been stipulated to be without warranty.
entity<|#|>Article 312<|#|>Content<|#|>A legal provision stating that a debtor may raise against the assignee the defenses he was entitled to raise against the assignor at the moment the assignment became effective, and may also raise defenses arising from the contract of assignment.

    *   **Identification:** Identify clearly defined and meaningful entities in the input text.
    *   **Entity Details:** For each identified entity, extract the following information:
        *   `entity_name`: The name of the entity. If the entity name is case-insensitive, capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case). Ensure **consistent naming** across the entire extraction process.
        *   `entity_type`: Categorize the entity using one of the following types: `Person,Creature,Organization,Location,Event,Concept,Method,Content,Data,Artifact,NaturalObject`. If none of the provided entity types apply, do not add new entity type and classify it as `Other`.
        *   `entity_description`: Provide a concise yet comprehensive description of the entity's attributes and activities, based *solely* on the information present in the input text.
    *   **Output Format - Entities:** Output a total of 4 fields for each entity, delimited by `<|#|>`, on a single line. The first field *must* be the literal string `entity`.
        *   Format: `entity<|#|>entity_name<|#|>entity_type<|#|>entity_description`

2.  **Relationship Extraction & Output:**
    *   **Identification:** Identify direct, clearly stated, and meaningful relationships between previously extracted entities.
    *   **N-ary Relationship Decomposition:** If a single statement describes a relationship involving more than two entities (an N-ary relationship), decompose it into multiple binary (two-entity) relationship pairs for separate description.
        *   **Example:** For "Alice, Bob, and Carol collaborated on Project X," extract binary relationships such as "Alice collaborated with Project X," "Bob collaborated with Project X," and "Carol collaborated with Project X," or "Alice collaborated with Bob," based on the most reasonable binary interpretations.
    *   **Relationship Details:** For each binary relationship, extract the following fields:
        *   `source_entity`: The name of the source entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `target_entity`: The name of the target entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `relationship_keywords`: One or more high-level keywords summarizing the overarching nature, concepts, or themes of the relationship. Multiple keywords within this field must be separated by a comma `,`. **DO NOT use `<|#|>` for separating multiple keywords within this field.**
        *   `relationship_description`: A concise explanation of the nature of the relationship between the source and target entities, providing a clear rationale for their connection.
    *   **Output Format - Relationships:** Output a total of 5 fields for each relationship, delimited by `<|#|>`, on a single line. The first field *must* be the literal string `relation`.
        *   Format: `relation<|#|>source_entity<|#|>target_entity<|#|>relationship_keywords<|#|>relationship_description`

3.  **Delimiter Usage Protocol:**
    *   The `<|#|>` is a complete, atomic marker and **must not be filled with content**. It serves strictly as a field separator.
    *   **Incorrect Example:** `entity<|#|>Tokyo<|location|>Tokyo is the capital of Japan.`
    *   **Correct Example:** `entity<|#|>Tokyo<|#|>location<|#|>Tokyo is the capital of Japan.`

4.  **Relationship Direction & Duplication:**
    *   Treat all relationships as **undirected** unless explicitly stated otherwise. Swapping the source and target entities for an undirected relationship does not constitute a new relationship.
    *   Avoid outputting duplicate relationships.

5.  **Output Order & Prioritization:**
    *   Output all extracted entities first, followed by all extracted relationships.
    *   Within the list of relationships, prioritize and output those relationships that are **most significant** to the core meaning of the input text first.

6.  **Context & Objectivity:**
    *   Ensure all entity names and descriptions are written in the **third person**.
    *   Explicitly name the subject or object; **avoid using pronouns** such as `this article`, `this paper`, `our company`, `I`, `you`, and `he/she`.

7.  **Language & Proper Nouns:**
    *   The entire output (entity names, keywords, and descriptions) must be written in `English`.
    *   Proper nouns (e.g., personal names, place names, organization names) should be retained in their original language if a proper, widely accepted translation is not available or would cause ambiguity.

8.  **Completion Signal:** Output the literal string `<|COMPLETE|>` only after all entities and relationships, following all criteria, have been completely extracted and outputted.

entity<|#|>Mandate (الوكالة)<|#|>Concept<|#|>A legal contract whereby one person (the mandator) authorizes another (the mandatary) to perform acts on their behalf. A general mandate confers only the power to perform acts of management, while a special mandate is required for acts beyond management such as sale, mortgage, gifts, arbitration, and court representation. A mandate is presumed gratuitous unless agreed otherwise, and it terminates by completion of work, expiration of period, or death of either party.
entity<|#|>Mandatary (الوكيل)<|#|>Person<|#|>The person appointed to perform a mandate. The mandatary is bound to execute the mandate without exceeding its limits, must exercise due care (varying by whether the mandate is gratuitous or remunerated), must inform the mandator of progress, render accounts, and may not use the mandator's property for personal benefit. Multiple mandataries may be jointly and severally liable under certain conditions.
entity<|#|>Mandator (الموكل)<|#|>Person<|#|>The person who gives a mandate to another. The mandator may revoke or restrict the mandate at any time, must repay expenses incurred by the mandatary with interest, is responsible for injury sustained by the mandatary in normal performance, and when several mandators appoint a sole mandatary for a common purpose, they are jointly and severally liable.
entity<|#|>Acts of Management<|#|>Concept<|#|>Acts that a mandatary may perform under a general mandate without special authorization, including granting leases of no more than three years, acts of preservation and maintenance, recovery of rights, discharge of debts, sale of perishable crops, goods or movables, and purchase of things necessary for preservation and exploitation of the mandate object.
entity<|#|>Special Mandate<|#|>Concept<|#|>A mandate required for any act that is not an act of management, in particular for sale, mortgage, gifts, compromise, admission, arbitration, tendering of an oath, and court representation. It only confers power to act in specified matters and matters necessarily incidental thereto according to prevailing custom.
entity<|#|>Substitute (نائب الوكيل)<|#|>Person<|#|>A person nominated by the mandatary to perform the mandate in the mandatary's place. If appointed without authorization, the mandatary is responsible for the substitute's acts as if they were their own, and both are jointly and severally liable. If authorized, the mandatary is only liable for faulty choice or faulty instructions.
entity<|#|>Third Party (الغير)<|#|>Person<|#|>An external person who deals with the mandatary or in whose interest a mandate may be granted. When a mandate is given in the interest of a third party, the mandator may not revoke or restrict it without the third party's consent. Articles 104 to 107 regarding representation apply to the relationship with third parties.
entity<|#|>Heirs (ورثة)<|#|>Person<|#|>The heirs of a deceased mandatary who, if they possess legal capacity and knowledge of the mandate, are bound to inform the mandator of the death and take necessary steps to protect the mandator's interests.
entity<|#|>Judge (القاضى)<|#|>Person<|#|>The judicial authority who assesses the remuneration agreed for a mandate, unless the remuneration has been voluntarily paid after performance of the mandate.
entity<|#|>Deposit (الوديعة)<|#|>Concept<|#|>A contract whereby one person (the depository) agrees to take delivery from another person (the depositor) a thing which the depository undertakes to keep in safe custody and return in kind. The depository may not use the deposited thing without authority or appoint a substitute except in cases of urgent necessity.
entity<|#|>Depository (المودع عنده)<|#|>Person<|#|>The person who receives the deposited thing and is bound to keep it in safe custody and return it. In a gratuitous deposit, the depository must exercise the care used in their own affairs; in a remunerated deposit, the diligence of a reasonable person is required. The depository must return the thing upon the depositor's request.
entity<|#|>Depositor (المودع)<|#|>Person<|#|>The person who delivers a thing to the depository for safe custody. The depositor has the right to demand return of the deposited thing at any time, unless the contract specifies a term fixed in the interests of the depository.
entity<|#|>Articles 104 to 107<|#|>Content<|#|>Legal provisions regarding representation that apply to the relationship of a mandator and a mandatary with third parties dealing with the mandatary, as referenced in Article 713.

1.  **Entity Extraction & Output:**
    *   **Identification:** Identify clearly defined and meaningful entities in the input text.
    *   **Entity Details:** For each identified entity, extract the following information:

        *   `entity_type`: Categorize the entity using one of the following types: `Person,Creature,Organization,Location,Event,Concept,Method,Content,Data,Artifact,NaturalObject`. If none of the provided entity types apply, do not add new entity type and classify it as `Other`.

        *   Format: `entity<|#|>entity_name<|#|>entity_type<|#|>entity_description`

2.  **Relationship Extraction & Output:**
    *   **Identification:** Identify direct, clearly stated, and meaningful relationships between previously extracted entities.
    *   **N-ary Relationship Decomposition:** If a single statement describes a relationship involving more than two entities (an N-ary relationship), decompose it into multiple binary (two-entity) relationship pairs for separate description.
        *   **Example:** For "Alice, Bob, and Carol collaborated on Project X," extract binary relationships such as "Alice collaborated with Project X," "Bob collaborated with Project X," and "Carol collaborated with Project X," or "Alice collaborated with Bob," based on the most reasonable binary interpretations.
    *   **Relationship Details:** For each binary relationship, extract the following fields:
        *   `source_entity`: The name of the source entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `target_entity`: The name of the target entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `relationship_keywords`: One or more high-level keywords summarizing the overarching nature, concepts, or themes of the relationship. Multiple keywords within this field must be separated by a comma `,`. **DO NOT use `<|#|>` for separating multiple keywords within this field.**
        *   `relationship_description`: A concise explanation of the nature of the relationship between the source and target entities, providing a clear rationale for their connection.
    *   **Output Format - Relationships:** Output a total of 5 fields for each relationship, delimited by `<|#|>`, on a single line. The first field *must* be the literal string `relation`.
        *   Format: `relation<|#|>source_entity<|#|>target_entity<|#|>relationship_keywords<|#|>relationship_description`

    *   Within the list of relationships, prioritize and output those relationships that are **most significant** to the core meaning of the input text first.

entity<|#|>Article 1144<|#|>Content<|#|>Article 1144 establishes that sums due to hotel proprietors by a traveller for accommodation, food, and expenses are secured by a privilege over the effects brought by the traveller to the hotel or its annexes, and that the hotel proprietor may object to removal of such effects if unpaid.
entity<|#|>Article 1145<|#|>Content<|#|>Article 1145 establishes that sums due to a vendor of a movable for price and accessories are secured by a privilege over the movable sold, enforceable as long as the movable preserves its identity, subject to third-party good faith rights and commercial provisions.
entity<|#|>Article 1146<|#|>Content<|#|>Article 1146 provides that co-owners who have partitioned a movable have a privilege over this movable for their respective remedies against each other resulting from partition and for repayment of any difference reverting to them.
entity<|#|>Article 1147<|#|>Content<|#|>Article 1147 establishes that the price and accessories due to a vendor of an immovable are secured by a privilege over the immovable sold, which must be inscribed and its rank is fixed by the date of inscription.
entity<|#|>Article 1148<|#|>Content<|#|>Article 1148 provides that sums due to contractors and architects entrusted with erection, reconstruction, repair, or maintenance of buildings or other works have a privilege over such works limited to the increase in value, and such privilege must be inscribed.
entity<|#|>Article 1149<|#|>Content<|#|>Article 1149 provides that co-owners who have partitioned an immovable have a privilege over it for their respective remedies against each other resulting from partition, including the right to claim payment of any difference, and such privilege must be inscribed.
entity<|#|>Hotel Proprietor<|#|>Person<|#|>A hotel proprietor who is owed sums for accommodation, food, and expenses by a traveller and holds a privilege over the effects brought by the traveller to the hotel or its annexes.
entity<|#|>Traveller<|#|>Person<|#|>A guest at a hotel who owes sums for accommodation, food, and expenses, and whose effects brought to the hotel are subject to the hotel proprietor's privilege.
entity<|#|>Vendor<|#|>Person<|#|>A seller of movable or immovable property who is owed the price and accessories and holds a privilege over the property sold.
entity<|#|>Lessor<|#|>Person<|#|>A person who leases property and holds a lessor's privilege, which has the same rank as a hotel proprietor's privilege.
entity<|#|>Co-owner<|#|>Person<|#|>A person who shares ownership of property with others and has partitioned it, holding a privilege over the partitioned property for remedies and repayment of differences.
entity<|#|>Contractor<|#|>Person<|#|>A person entrusted with the erection, reconstruction, repair, or maintenance of buildings or other works, entitled to a privilege over such works.
entity<|#|>Architect<|#|>Person<|#|>A person entrusted with the construction or design of buildings or other works, entitled to a privilege over such works.
entity<|#|>Hotel Proprietor's Privilege<|#|>Concept<|#|>A legal privilege securing sums due to hotel proprietors over effects brought by travellers, having the same rank as a lessor's privilege, enforceable even on effects not owned by the traveller provided they are not lost or stolen property.
entity<|#|>Vendor's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>Concept<|#|>A legal privilege securing sums due to a vendor of movable property over the thing sold, ranking below other movable privileges but enforceable against lessors and hotel proprietors if they had knowledge of the privilege at the time the movable was brought onto their premises.
entity<|#|>Vendor's Privilege Over Immovable<|#|>Concept<|#|>A legal privilege securing sums due to a vendor of an immovable over the property sold, requiring inscription notwithstanding transcription of the sale, with rank fixed by the date of inscription.
entity<|#|>Co-partitioner's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>Concept<|#|>A legal privilege held by co-owners over partitioned movables for remedies against each other resulting from partition and for repayment of differences, having the same rank as a vendor's privilege.
entity<|#|>Co-partitioner's Privilege Over Immovable<|#|>Concept<|#|>A legal privilege held by co-owners over partitioned immovables for remedies and payment of differences, requiring inscription with rank fixed by the date of inscription.
entity<|#|>Contractor's And Architect's Privilege<|#|>Concept<|#|>A legal privilege securing sums due to contractors and architects over buildings or works they erected, reconstructed, repaired, or maintained, limited to the increase in value resulting from such works, requiring inscription.
entity<|#|>Lessor's Privilege<|#|>Concept<|#|>A legal privilege held by a lessor over leased property, having the same rank as a hotel proprietor's privilege.
entity<|#|>Inscription<|#|>Method<|#|>A legal requirement for registration of certain privileges over immovables, which determines the rank of the privilege by the date of its registration.
entity<|#|>Third Party In Good Faith<|#|>Concept<|#|>A third party who acquires rights over property without knowledge of existing privileges, whose acquired rights are protected against enforcement of such privileges.
entity<|#|>Special Privileges Over Immovables<|#|>Concept<|#|>A category of legal privileges applicable to immovable property, encompassing the vendor's privilege, the contractor's and architect's privilege, and the co-partitioner's privilege over immovables.
relation<|#|>Article 1144<|#|>Hotel Proprietor's Privilege<|#|>legal provision, establishment<|#|>Article 1144 establishes the hotel proprietor's privilege over effects brought by a traveller to secure sums due for accommodation, food, and expenses.
relation<|#|>Article 1145<|#|>Vendor's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>legal provision, establishment<|#|>Article 1145 establishes the vendor's privilege over movable property sold to secure the price and accessories due.
relation<|#|>Article 1146<|#|>Co-partitioner's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>legal provision, establishment<|#|>Article 1146 establishes the co-partitioner's privilege over partitioned movables for remedies and repayment of differences.
relation<|#|>Article 1147<|#|>Vendor's Privilege Over Immovable<|#|>legal provision, establishment<|#|>Article 1147 establishes the vendor's privilege over immovable property sold to secure the price and accessories due.
relation<|#|>Article 1148<|#|>Contractor's And Architect's Privilege<|#|>legal provision, establishment<|#|>Article 1148 establishes the contractor's and architect's privilege over buildings or works to secure sums due for construction, repair, or maintenance.
relation<|#|>Article 1149<|#|>Co-partitioner's Privilege Over Immovable<|#|>legal provision, establishment<|#|>Article 1149 establishes the co-partitioner's privilege over partitioned immovables for remedies and payment of differences.
relation<|#|>Hotel Proprietor<|#|>Traveller<|#|>debt, service relationship<|#|>The hotel proprietor is owed sums by the traveller for accommodation, food, and expenses incurred on the traveller's account.
relation<|#|>Hotel Proprietor<|#|>Hotel Proprietor's Privilege<|#|>holder, beneficiary<|#|>The hotel proprietor is the holder and beneficiary of the hotel proprietor's privilege over the traveller's effects.
relation<|#|>Vendor<|#|>Vendor's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>holder, beneficiary<|#|>The vendor of movable property holds a privilege over the movable sold to secure the price and accessories.
relation<|#|>Vendor<|#|>Vendor's Privilege Over Immovable<|#|>holder, beneficiary<|#|>The vendor of immovable property holds a privilege over the immovable sold to secure the price and accessories.
relation<|#|>Co-owner<|#|>Co-partitioner's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>holder, beneficiary<|#|>Co-owners who partitioned a movable hold a privilege over it to secure their remedies against each other.
relation<|#|>Co-owner<|#|>Co-partitioner's Privilege Over Immovable<|#|>holder, beneficiary<|#|>Co-owners who partitioned an immovable hold a privilege over it to secure their remedies and payment of differences.
relation<|#|>Contractor<|#|>Contractor's And Architect's Privilege<|#|>holder, beneficiary<|#|>The contractor holds a privilege over buildings or works to secure sums due for construction, reconstruction, repair, or maintenance work.
relation<|#|>Architect<|#|>Contractor's And Architect's Privilege<|#|>holder, beneficiary<|#|>The architect holds a privilege over buildings or works to secure sums due for design and construction-related work.
relation<|#|>Lessor<|#|>Lessor's Privilege<|#|>holder, beneficiary<|#|>The lessor holds a lessor's privilege over leased property.
relation<|#|>Hotel Proprietor's Privilege<|#|>Lessor's Privilege<|#|>rank equivalence, priority<|#|>The hotel proprietor's privilege has the same rank as the lessor's privilege; if both claims compete, the first in date has priority.
relation<|#|>Co-partitioner's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>Vendor's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>rank equivalence, priority<|#|>The co-partitioner's privilege over movable has the same rank as the vendor's privilege over movable; if both compete, the first in date has priority.
relation<|#|>Vendor's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>Lessor<|#|>enforceability, knowledge requirement<|#|>The vendor's privilege over movable operates against the lessor if it can be proved the lessor had knowledge of the privilege when the movable was brought onto the leased property.
relation<|#|>Vendor's Privilege Over Movable<|#|>Hotel Proprietor<|#|>enforceability, knowledge requirement<|#|>The vendor's privilege over movable operates against the hotel proprietor if it can be proved the hotel proprietor had knowledge of the privilege when the movable was brought into the hotel.

A Creditor (الدائن) is a person or party to whom a debt, obligation, or annuity is owed and who is entitled to receive payment or performance from a debtor. The creditor holds a range of rights and powers in relation to the obligation, including the authority to ratify or refuse an assignment of debt, to accept payment, and to demand specific performance of the obligation. Where payment is not due, the creditor may be required to make restitution, with the right to restitution influenced by whether the payment was received in good faith. A creditor may also voluntarily release the debtor or be replaced through novation by a third party.

To protect and enforce their rights, a creditor may take legal proceedings against the debtor, seek court orders for enforcement, and claim damages for losses and lost profits. The creditor may interrupt prescription through legal proceedings, summons, attachment, or other formal acts. A creditor is entitled to require the debtor to provide adequate securities guaranteeing the debt and may take protective measures when there are reasonable grounds to apprehend misappropriation — for instance, under Article 1133, a creditor may apply for movables charged with a privilege in their favor to be placed in judicial custody. The creditor benefits from pledges, mortgages, and other forms of security, and may apply for a judgment charge on the debtor's immovable property, with the right to appeal a rejection of such application to the Court of First Instance. Creditors are ranked by priority for payment from the proceeds of property sales.

In relation to sureties, the creditor receives the guarantee from the surety but must generally first take proceedings against the debtor before pursuing the surety. The creditor is bound to prove the debt in bankruptcy to preserve rights against the surety, and may levy execution on the property of both the debtor and, under certain conditions, the surety.

During insolvency proceedings, creditors retain certain rights, including the ability to bring individual actions against the debtor. These rights are preserved even upon the cessation of insolvency.

The Purchaser is the buyer in a sale contract who acquires ownership of a thing in consideration of a price. As a party to the sale, the Purchaser is obligated to pay the price and take delivery of the thing sold, bearing the costs of the deed of sale, stamp duties, transcription fees, and delivery expenses unless otherwise agreed. The Purchaser must have sufficient acquaintance with the thing sold and is obligated to inspect it for defects upon delivery, giving timely notice of any discovered defects. In trial or tasting sales, the Purchaser has the right to accept or refuse the thing sold.

The Purchaser is entitled to significant protections under the law. These include warranty protection against defects, disturbance, and dispossession. When disturbed in enjoyment or threatened with dispossession, the Purchaser may retain the price. The Purchaser is also entitled to claim compensation, refunds, legal interest, and reimbursement of expenses in cases of dispossession or defects.

In specific contexts, the Purchaser's role carries additional legal implications. When purchasing mortgaged immovable property, the Purchaser may agree with the vendor to assume the mortgage debt through assignment, with the creditor required to ratify or refuse within six months of notification. When a Purchaser buys an industrial or commercial establishment from a lessee on leased property, the court may maintain the lease in the Purchaser's favor despite a prohibition on sub-letting, provided the Purchaser furnishes adequate security and the lessor suffers no real prejudice. A Purchaser who buys a deposited thing from the heir of a depository in good faith is also recognized as a protected party. In property transactions subject to preemption rights, the Purchaser must be notified of any intention to exercise preemption, and the preemptor may assume the Purchaser's rights and obligations.

The Court is the judicial body vested with broad authority across civil, contractual, property, and estate matters. It serves as the primary judicial authority empowered to authorize deposits, public auctions, and judicial custody, as well as to grant reasonable delays for the performance of obligations. In the realm of contracts, the Court decides points of detail in disputes according to the nature of the transaction, the provisions of law, custom, and equity. It may order the nullity of a void contract on its own initiative and, in cases of economic imbalance caused by exceptional events, it has the authority to reduce compensation due for loss of profit, grant price increases, or order the resiliation of the contract.

The Court exercises significant powers over personal status and capacity. It pronounces or raises interdictions, appoints judicial advisers, and ratifies acts of minors and interdicted persons. It also adjudicates avoidance claims and is authorized to grant revocation of a gift and adjudicate on the nullity of partnership deeds. In partnership matters specifically, the Court may order dissolution, appoint liquidators, and authorize a partner's retirement upon application.

In property and lease matters, the Court authorizes preventive measures against building dangers, adjudicates claims, and its involvement triggers obligations such as restitution of profits. It may maintain a lease despite a prohibition on sub-letting when a commercial or industrial establishment is sold, grant the lessor time for settlement of payments for improvements, and authorize the lessee to carry out repairs and deduct costs from rent when the lessor delays maintenance obligations. The Court also grants damages instead of material redress for breaches of servitude restrictions when it considers there are reasons for doing so, and decides matters in accordance with equity when movables belonging to different owners become mingled. It handles actions in preemption before the district court where the property is situated.

Regarding co-ownership and joint property, the Court resolves disputes among co-owners, appoints managers for commonly held property, orders security for dissenting co-owners, and decides on the alienation of jointly owned property. It may authorize a co-owner to withdraw a share from family joint ownership before the agreed term, discharge a manager, order the sale of a lower storey, and appoint a representative of a syndicate.

The Court oversees the entire estate administration process, including receiving inventory filings, investigating disputes, authorizing debt payments, fixing deadlines, ordering the sale or allocation of property, and issuing inheritance certificates. It is also the body before which conditions of sale are filed and where third party holders or applicants deposit sums to cover costs or satisfy creditors. Additionally, the Court renders orders authorizing judgment charges, and its greffier is responsible for notifying and endorsing such orders. The Court orders judicial custody, stamps receiver account books, and receives copies of accounts from court-appointed receivers.

Public Auction is a legally governed sale method conducted in accordance with formal statutory provisions and judicial authorization. It serves as the prescribed or required mechanism in several distinct legal contexts, including the liquidation of movable and immovable property belonging to an estate—carried out following the manner and delays established for forced sales unless all heirs unanimously agree to an alternative method—as well as the forced sale of mortgaged immovable property through compulsory expropriation formalities, which may be initiated either by a creditor's application or by a third-party holder's wish to purge the mortgage. A mortgaged property must be marketable and susceptible to sale by public auction for this mechanism to apply.

Public Auction also functions as a court-authorized method for the sale of pledged property, particularly when the pledged item is deteriorating, in danger of perishing, or when there is a default of payment, as referenced in Articles 1119, 1121, and 1129. Only movables or immovables that can be sold independently may become the object of a pledge under this framework, as stated in Article 1097. Additionally, it is the designated sale method for items of a rapidly perishing nature or movables that incur exorbitant storage costs, with the proceeds from such sales deposited in the Caisse du Tribunal.

Several legal consequences attach specifically to sales conducted by Public Auction. A contract is formed only upon acceptance of the final bid, and any prior bid is nullified from the moment a higher bid is made, even if that higher bid is subsequently found to be void. Because a Public Auction is conducted in conformity with legal provisions, an action for supplement of price on grounds of lesion does not lie. Furthermore, preemption rights cannot be exercised when the sale is made by Public Auction, as explicitly stated in Article 939.

In legal contexts, a Third Party is any person or entity who is not an original party to a contract, agreement, or legal obligation between two primary parties. The concept of a Third Party arises across a wide range of civil and contractual situations, consistently referring to an external participant whose rights, obligations, and interactions with the primary parties are governed by specific legal provisions.

In the realm of obligations and contracts, a Third Party may assume the role of a new debtor or a new creditor through the mechanism of novation, as described in Article 352. A Third Party may also make payment on behalf of a debtor and, upon doing so, may be subrogated into the rights of the creditor. However, while a Third Party may acquire rights under a contract through a stipulation for a Third Party—gaining a direct right against the promisor—they generally do not acquire obligations under a contract to which they are not a party. A Third Party may also serve as a beneficiary of consideration under Article 497 or as a debtor in the contribution of debts under Article 513, and may be affected by partnership publication formalities under Article 506.

In property-related matters, a Third Party may hold an existing right over a thing sold at the time of sale, which is enforceable against the purchaser and may cause disturbance in the purchaser's enjoyment. A Third Party may also acquire possession of property, such as a good-faith purchaser at a market or public sale, and may be subject to restitution claims. Additionally, in the context of property disposition, the lawful interest and lifetime of a Third Party—being a person other than the one disposing of property or the one in whose favor it is disposed—may serve as valid grounds for an inalienability clause under Article 823.

With respect to security interests, a Third Party is a person not party to a mortgage agreement; a mortgage is effective against Third Parties only if the deed or judgment establishing the mortgage has been inscribed before the Third Party acquires real rights on the property, subject to bankruptcy provisions. Similarly, in the context of a pledge, a Third Party may be chosen by the contracting parties to hold the pledged thing, and their rights are preserved under the law even as the pledge confers rights against all persons.

A Third Party may also play a role in matters of lease, where an external party may claim rights over the leased property or commit trespass or disturbance. In such cases, the lessee may take legal action against the Third Party in the lessee's own name for damages and possessory actions. Furthermore, a Third Party who is not a contracting party may practice fraudulent misrepresentation or duress; the victim of such Third Party acts may demand avoidance of the contract only if the other contracting party was aware or should have been aware of the fraud or duress, as specified in Articles 126 and 128.

A Debtor (المدين) is the person or party legally obligated to fulfill, perform, or pay a debt or obligation to a creditor. The debtor's core duty is to deliver or perform the object of an obligation, and may be compelled to specific performance. When the degree of quality of the object is unspecified and cannot be determined by usage or circumstances, the debtor must supply an article of average quality. In monetary obligations, the debtor is bound only to the actual figure stated in the contract. The debtor is always liable for fraud or gross negligence and may be held liable for damages upon non-performance or delay. The debtor enjoys several rights, including the designation of which debt to discharge, the right to demand receipts, the right to make a judicial deposit, and the right of retraction of tender under specified conditions. In alternative obligations, the debtor holds election rights. A debtor cannot claim restitution of voluntary payments made to discharge a natural obligation.

The debtor may invoke defenses against an assignee that were available against the assignor, as well as defenses arising from the contract of assignment. The debtor may also invoke prescription as a defense, and may interrupt prescription by expressly or tacitly acknowledging the debt. In the case of a litigious right that has been assigned, the debtor may extinguish the assigned right by paying the assignee the actual price paid, together with expenses and interest. The debtor may be replaced through novation or delegation by a third party. Revocation of a third-party stipulation does not liberate the debtor vis-à-vis the stipulator unless expressly agreed.

In the context of mortgages and secured obligations, the debtor is the person obligated to pay the secured debt underlying the mortgage. The mortgagor may be the debtor or a third party acting in the debtor's interest. If mortgaged property perishes or deteriorates without the mortgagor's fault, the debtor may either furnish adequate security or pay the debt in full before it falls due. After the debt has fallen due, the debtor may transfer the mortgaged property to the creditor in payment of the debt. The debtor's property may also be subject to privileged rights, including general and special privileges covering obligations such as wages, alimony, taxes, and rent, and may be subject to execution to satisfy outstanding debts, expropriation proceedings, and judgment charges. The debtor may lodge an appeal against an order authorizing a judgment charge before the judge who gave the order or before the Court of First Instance.

A debtor who holds the right of redemption under an annuity may be compelled to redeem if payment defaults occur, securities prove insufficient, or insolvency arises. In the context of suretyship, the debtor's failure to perform triggers the surety's obligation, and the debtor may be required to offer a solvent surety residing in Egypt or adequate real security. If the debtor becomes bankrupt, the creditor must prove the debt.

A debtor may be declared bankrupt or insolvent if assets are insufficient to meet obligations, and is subject to penalties for willful insolvency or the concealment of property. Insolvency may result in the forfeiture of term benefits. Upon cessation of insolvency, the debtor may reclaim previously discharged debts.

Good Faith is a foundational legal principle requiring that parties act honestly, fairly, and without fraud in their legal dealings. At its core, it binds contracting parties not only to the express terms of their agreements but also to everything deemed a necessary sequel according to law, usage, and equity. Good faith operates as both a general standard of conduct and a specific legal state of mind applied across a wide range of civil law contexts.

In the realm of contractual obligations, good faith governs the performance of contracts and the handling of mistakes. A party who has committed a mistake cannot exploit it in a manner contrary to good faith, and the mistaken party remains bound by the intended contract if the other party is prepared to perform it. Good faith also serves as a legal condition enabling creditors and particular successors in title to avail themselves of a hidden contract or to establish the simulation of a contract by which they were prejudiced.

In property and possession law, good faith describes an honest belief in the legitimacy of one's possession at the time of acquisition. A possessor acting in good faith is one who is unaware of infringing upon another's right, and this state is always presumed by law. Good faith possession serves as a basis for acquiring ownership and fruits, limits liability for loss or deterioration, and affects the duration required for acquisitive prescription. Among multiple lessees competing for the same property, a lessee who in good faith transcribes a lease before another takes possession obtains preference. Good faith is also evaluated by courts when resolving disputes over mingled movables in accordance with the rules of equity.

Good faith extends significant protections to third parties and creditors. A third party who acquires a real right on an immovable in good faith is shielded from the supplement of price action. Similarly, a purchaser who acknowledges or compromises with a third party's claim while acting in good faith preserves warranty rights. In mortgage law, a mortgage constituted by an owner whose title is later annulled, resiliated, or abolished remains valid in favor of a mortgagee creditor who acted in good faith at the time of the mortgage's conclusion. Good faith also protects third parties acquiring rights during the interval between the extinguishment and revival of a mortgage, and is a required state of honest belief for a creditor seeking a judgment charge over immovable property.

In the context of unjust enrichment and payment, a good faith recipient of undue payment is bound only to return what was actually received, reflecting the law's recognition that honest conduct should limit the scope of restitutionary liability.

The Judge (القاضي) is a judicial authority and officer vested with broad discretionary powers across numerous areas of civil law. As the primary judicial decision-maker, the Judge is responsible for deciding cases using various sources of law and determining the applicable law in matters involving persons of unknown or plural nationality.

In procedural and prescription matters, the Judge may not invoke prescription on his own initiative but may direct oaths in one-year prescription cases and presides over all legal proceedings related to prescription. The Judge also has authority to grant extensions of time, such as allowing administrators additional time to file inventory statements when justified by circumstances.

In the realm of contractual and obligations law, the Judge plays a central role. The Judge may grant additional time to debtors, reject rescission applications for minor breaches, and assess damages in light of prevailing circumstances while determining the appropriate method of compensation. The Judge is empowered to reduce excessively onerous contractual obligations arising from exceptional and unpredictable events, modify leonine conditions in contracts of adhesion, and reduce obligations to reasonable limits. Under Article 224, the Judge may also reduce the amount of damages agreed upon between contracting parties. Furthermore, the Judge fixes reasonable times for the term of obligations, determines the object of obligations when parties fail to elect, and adjudicates matters related to insolvency and conditional obligations.

Regarding damages, penalties, and natural obligations, the Judge determines the existence of natural obligations in the absence of legal provisions, orders specific performance, fixes damages, and authorizes enforcement actions. The Judge may increase penalties or reduce damages based on circumstances, including reducing damages for a voluntary agent's mistakes when justified. In cases of dispossession where the donor intentionally concealed the cause, the Judge may award equitable compensation to the donee.

In partnership and corporate matters, the Judge evaluates the seriousness of reasons for dissolution, appoints liquidators when partners cannot agree, and authorizes a partner's retirement from a partnership. The Judge also oversees wakf (waqf) property matters, specifically authorizing leases exceeding three years and supervising the Nazir's leasing activities, with the Nazir required to obtain the Judge's permission for such long-term leases.

The Judge exercises authority over judicial custody, appointing receivers, reducing excessive betting stakes, and making decisions regarding the termination and administration of custody arrangements. In employment and remuneration matters, the Judge fixes salaries in accordance with equity when no applicable rates or customs exist, determines the nature and extent of work to be performed, and may designate a trustworthy person to receive information necessary to verify the accuracy of a master's profit-sharing account on behalf of a worker.

In property and structural matters, the Judge is empowered under Article 962 to order the suspension or continuance of threatening works and to require adequate guarantees. Under Articles 859 and 860, the Judge may order the sale of a lower storey, order the execution of urgent repairs, and enforce structural obligations between storey owners. The Judge also determines the method of repayment of expenses in usufruct arrangements, may order the removal of property from a usufructuary, and may declare the extinction of a usufruct. In mortgage matters, the Judge fixes the portion of property to which a mortgage is transferred after partition and may order the cessation of acts that could result in loss or deterioration of mortgaged property. Additionally, under Article 1000, the Judge may be delegated by the President of the Court to draw up a hekr deed.

The (Creditor, Debtor) relation describes the fundamental legal and financial relationship in which a Debtor owes an obligation or debt to a Creditor, who is entitled to receive payment or performance from the Debtor. The Debtor is obligated to fulfill the debt to the Creditor or the Creditor's representative, and this relationship is governed by rules on enforceability, restitution, and premature payment. The Creditor may refuse performance by a person other than the Debtor when the contract or the nature of the obligation requires personal performance.

The Creditor possesses a broad range of rights and remedies to protect and enforce the obligation. The Creditor may take protective measures, demand security, and initiate legal proceedings against the Debtor to recover the debt. Through an enforceable judgment, the Creditor may obtain judgment charges on the Debtor's immovable property, and both parties hold mutual rights to appeal orders related to such judgment charges before the Court of First Instance. The Creditor may also apply for judicial custody of the Debtor's movables charged with a privilege when there are reasonable grounds to fear misappropriation, as provided under Article 1133. When a surety is involved, the Creditor must first take proceedings against the Debtor before pursuing the surety and must prove the debt in bankruptcy to preserve rights against the surety.

On the Debtor's side, the Debtor must provide any promised securities to the Creditor and may be compelled to redeem an annuity upon failure to pay for two consecutive years or upon insolvency. The Debtor may also be subject to insolvency proceedings initiated by the Creditor. However, the Debtor retains certain rights, including the ability to interrupt the running of prescription by expressly or tacitly acknowledging the debt.

# Egyptian Law on Contracts

Based on the Egyptian Civil Code (القانون المدني المصري), contracts are governed by comprehensive rules covering their formation, validity, effects, and various types. Below is a detailed overview:

---

## 1. Formation of Contracts (Consent / الرضاء)

A **contract is formed** when two parties exchange matching expressions of intention, subject to any special formalities required by law (Article 89) [1].

### Expression of Intention
- An intention may be declared **verbally, in writing, by commonly used signs**, or by conduct that leaves no doubt as to its meaning (Article 90) [1].
- A declaration becomes effective when it reaches the person to whom it was addressed (Article 91) [1].

### Offer and Acceptance
- If a **time limit** is fixed for acceptance, the offeror is bound to maintain the offer until the expiration of that time limit (Article 93) [1].
- If an offer is made **during a meeting** (in person or by telephone) without a time limit, the offeror is released if acceptance is not immediate (Article 94) [1].
- Acceptance that goes beyond, restricts, or modifies the offer is considered a **rejection comprising a new offer** (Article 96) [1].
- Contracts between absent parties are deemed concluded at the place and time the offeror becomes aware of the acceptance (Article 97) [1].
- **Silence** may be equivalent to acceptance when there are prior dealings between the parties or when the offer is solely in the interest of the offeree (Article 98) [1].

### Earnest Money (Araboun / العربون)
Payment of earnest money at the time of the contract indicates that either party may withdraw. The party who paid forfeits it upon withdrawal; the party who received it must repay **double** upon withdrawal (Article 103) [1].

---

## 2. Capacity to Contract (الأهلية)

- **Every person** who has not been declared under total or partial legal incapacity has the legal capacity to contract (Article 109) [1].
- A **minor lacking discretion** (under 7 years old): all legal acts are **void** (Article 110) [1].
- A **minor possessing discretion**: acts that are wholly beneficial are valid; acts wholly detrimental are void; acts that are mixed are **voidable** in the interest of the minor (Article 111) [1].
- A minor who has attained **18 years** and is authorized to manage property may validly perform acts of management within legal limits (Article 112) [1].
- Acts by persons suffering from **insanity or mental derangement** are null if made after registration of the interdiction sentence; before registration, they are null only if the condition was commonly known (Article 114) [1].

---

## 3. Vices of Consent (عيب الإرادة)

### Mistake (الغلط)
- A party may demand avoidance of a contract for an **essential mistake** — one of such gravity that the party would not have contracted without it (Article 121) [1].
- A mistake is deemed essential particularly when it relates to a **quality of the thing** considered essential, or to the **identity or qualities of the person** with whom the contract was made (Article 121) [1].
- Mistakes in law may also entitle avoidance if they fulfill the elements of a mistake of fact (Article 122) [1].
- Mere **errors of calculation or clerical errors** do not affect validity but must be corrected (Article 123) [1].

### Fraudulent Misrepresentation (التدليس)
- A contract may be avoided if the **artifices** practiced by one party are of such gravity that the other party would not have contracted without them (Article 125) [1].
- **Intentional silence** about a fact or circumstance also constitutes fraudulent misrepresentation (Article 125) [1].

### Duress (الإكراه)
- A contract is voidable if one party contracted under **justifiable fear** unlawfully instilled by the other party (Article 127) [1].
- Fear is justified when the party was led to believe that a serious and imminent danger threatened life, limb, honor, or property (Article 127) [1].
- The **sex, age, social position, and health** of the victim are taken into account in assessing duress (Article 127) [1].

### Lesion / Exploitation (الغلاء الاستغلالي)
- If obligations are grossly disproportionate, and one party exploited the other's **levity of character or unbridled passion**, the judge may annul or reduce the obligations (Article 129) [1].
- The action must be brought within **one year** from the date of the contract (Article 129) [1].

---

## 4. Object of the Obligation (محل الالتزام)

- The object must be **possible, determinate (at least as to kind and quantity), lawful**, and not contrary to public policy or morality (Articles 132, 133, 135) [1].
- Agreements regarding the **succession of a living person** are void except where the law provides otherwise (Article 131) [1].
- If the object is **money**, the debtor is bound only to the figure stated, regardless of fluctuations in value (Article 134) [1].

---

## 5. Consideration / Cause (السبب)

- A contract is void if an obligation is assumed **without consideration** or for consideration contrary to public policy or morality (Article 136) [1].
- An obligation is presumed to have **lawful consideration**, even if not expressed, unless the contrary is proved (Article 137) [1].

---

## 6. Nullity (البطلان)

### Voidable Contracts (قابل للإبطال)
- The right of avoidance belongs only to the **specifically protected party** (Article 138) [1].
- This right is extinguished by **express or implied ratification**, which is retroactive (Article 139) [1].
- The right is prescribed if not invoked within **3 years** from the relevant triggering event, and in no case beyond **15 years** from the contract date (Article 140) [1].

### Absolutely Void Contracts (باطل)
- Any interested person may invoke nullity, and the court may order it **on its own initiative** (Article 141) [1].
- Nullity proceedings are prescribed after **15 years** from the date of the contract (Article 141) [1].

### Effects of Nullity
- The parties are **reinstated to their original position**; if impossible, equivalent damages may be awarded (Article 142) [1].
- A person without capacity who causes annulment is only liable to refund **profits actually derived** (Article 142) [1].
- If only part of a contract is void, that part alone is annulled unless the contract would not have been made without it (Article 143) [1].

---

## 7. Effects of Contracts (آثار العقد)

- **The contract is the law of the parties** — it can only be revoked or altered by mutual consent or for reasons provided by law (Article 147) [1].
- Contracts must be performed in **good faith** and in accordance with their contents (Article 148) [1].
- Effects extend to **universal successors** (heirs) unless the contract, nature of the transaction, or law provides otherwise (Article 145) [1].
- Obligations relating to property also bind **particular successors** if they constitute essential elements and the successor had knowledge (Article 146) [1].

### Exceptional Circumstances (الظروف الاستثنائية)
- If exceptional and unforeseeable events make performance **excessively onerous**, the judge may reduce the obligation to reasonable limits (Article 147(2)) [1].

### Contracts of Adhesion (عقود الإذعان)
- If such contracts contain **leonine (oppressive) conditions**, the judge may modify or relieve the adhering party of them (Article 149) [1].
- Obscure clauses in contracts of adhesion must not be interpreted to the detriment of the adhering party (Article 151) [1].

### Stipulation for Third Parties (الاشتراط لمصلحة الغير)
- A contract does not create obligations for third parties but **may create rights** in their favor (Article 152) [1].
- A person may stipulate an obligation for the benefit of a third party if he has a personal interest (material or moral) in its performance (Article 154) [1].
- The third party acquires a **direct right** against the promisor (Article 154) [1].

### Interpretation of Contracts
- If the wording is **clear**, it cannot be deviated from (Article 150) [1].
- If interpretation is needed, the **common intention** of the parties must be sought, beyond the literal meaning (Article 150) [1].
- **Doubt is construed in favor of the debtor** (Article 151) [1].

---

## 8. Representation (النيابة)

- A contract entered into by a **representative within his authority** in the name of the principal produces effects for the principal (Article 105) [1].
- No person may contract with himself in the name of the person he represents without the principal's authority (Article 108) [1].
- The representative's knowledge and vices of will (not the principal's) are what count, unless the representative acted on specific instructions (Article 104) [1].

---

## 9. Types of Contracts

The Civil Code also governs specific types of contracts, including:

- **Sale (البيع)** — including sale of another's property, litigious rights, inheritances, and sale during last illness (Articles 462–481) [1].
- **Exchange (المقايضة)** — governed by the rules of sale to the extent compatible with its nature (Articles 482–485) [1].
- **Gift (الهبة)** — must be made by authentic document (for immovables) or by delivery (for movables); gifts of future property are void (Articles 486–492) [1].

---

### References

- [1] Egyptian Law (القانون المدني المصري)

# Personal Status and Family Law in the Egyptian Civil Code

The Egyptian Civil Code addresses several key areas of personal status and family law, spanning legal personality, capacity, marriage, divorce, inheritance, guardianship, and alimony. Below is a comprehensive summary of the rules as found in the provided context.

---

## 1. Legal Personality and Capacity

**Legal personality** commences from the moment a child is **born alive** and ends at **death**. The law also determines the rights of an unborn child (*en ventre de sa mère*), as established in **Article 29** [1].

Birth and death are established through **official registers** kept for that purpose. Where such registers are unavailable or inaccurate, proof may be established by any other means (**Article 30**) [1].

### Degrees of Legal Capacity

The Code establishes a tiered system of legal capacity:

- **Full legal capacity** is attained at **twenty-one years of age** (Gregorian calendar), provided the person is in possession of mental faculties and not under legal disability (**Article 44**) [1].
- **Devoid of discretion**: A person who has not attained the age of **seven** is considered devoid of discretion and incapable of exercising civil rights. This also applies to persons suffering from feeble-mindedness or insanity (**Article 45**) [1].
- **Limited legal capacity** applies to persons who have reached the age of discretion but not majority, and to adults who are prodigals or imbeciles (**Article 46**) [1].
- Persons deprived of full or partial legal capacity are governed by rules of **natural or legal guardianship, curatorship**, and other protective systems (**Article 47**) [1].

Importantly, **no person may renounce their legal capacity or modify its rules** (Article 48), nor may a person renounce their personal liberty (Article 49) [1].

---

## 2. Marriage

### Conditions of Validity

The fundamental conditions relating to the **validity of marriage** are governed by the **national law of each spouse** individually (**Article 12**) [1].

### Effects of Marriage

The **effects of marriage**, including its effects upon the property of the spouses, are regulated by the **law of the country to which the husband belongs at the time of conclusion of the marriage** (**Article 13**) [1].

### Egyptian Law Override

If **one of the spouses is Egyptian** at the time of the marriage, **Egyptian law alone shall apply** — except as regards the legal capacity to marry (**Article 14**) [1].

---

## 3. Divorce, Separation, and Repudiation

The Code distinguishes between three modes of ending a marriage:

- **Repudiation**: Governed by the law of the country to which the **husband belongs at the time of repudiation**.
- **Divorce (التطليق)** and **Separation (الانفصال)**: Both are governed by the law of the country to which the **husband belongs at the time of commencement of the legal proceedings** (**Article 13**) [1].

---

## 4. Alimony (النفقة)

Obligations for the **payment of alimony between relatives** are governed by the **national law of the person liable** for such payment (**Article 15**) [1]. Where the debtor is Egyptian, Egyptian law applies.

---

## 5. Guardianship and Protective Systems (الولاية والوصاية والقوامة)

All fundamental matters relating to **natural and legal guardianship, receivership, and other forms of protection** for persons without legal capacity and absent persons are governed by the **national law of the person who should be protected** (**Article 16**) [1].

The **domicile** of a minor, a person under legal disability, a missing person, or an absent person is the domicile of their **legal representative**. However, a minor who has attained eighteen years may have a special domicile for acts they are legally capable of performing (**Article 42**) [1].

---

## 6. Inheritance and Wills (الميراث والوصية)

### Governing Law

- **Inheritance, wills, and other dispositions taking effect after death** are governed by the **national law of the deceased (de cujus), the testator, or the person disposing of property at the time of death** (**Article 17(1)**) [1].
- The **form of a will** is governed by either the national law of the testator **at the time the will is made**, or the law of the country **where the will is made** (**Article 17(2)**) [1].

### Substantive Rules

- **Wills** are further governed by **Mohammedan (Islamic) Law** and specific legislation on wills (Article 915) [1].
- A disposition made to an heir is deemed **testamentary** when the disposer retains possession and enjoyment of the property during his lifetime (**Article 917**) [1].
- **Property not included in a division** devolves in common upon the heirs in accordance with the **rules of inheritance** (**Article 910**) [1].
- Any heir may **call for a division of the estate** where estate debts are unresolved or creditors do not agree (**Article 913**, referencing Article 895) [1].

---

## 7. Family Relationships

The Code defines the family of a person as being composed of his **relatives** — persons having a common ascendant (**Article 34**) [1]. It further distinguishes:

- **Direct lineal relationship**: between ascendants and descendants.
- **Collateral relationship**: between persons who share a common ancestor without one being a descendant of the other.

Degrees of relationship are calculated by counting each relative when ascending to the common ancestor (**Articles 35–36**) [1]. The relatives of either spouse are deemed to be relatives of the other spouse in the same line and degree (**Article 37**) [1].

---

## 8. Name and Personality Rights

Every person must have a **first name and a family name**, with the family name bestowed upon children (**Article 38**) [1]. A person whose name is unlawfully disputed or used by another has the right to demand cessation and compensation (**Article 51**) [1]. More broadly, any person whose inherent personality rights are unlawfully infringed may seek cessation and damages (**Article 50**) [1].

---

## 9. Family Joint Ownership

Members of the **same family** who share a **common occupation or interest** may agree in writing to create a **family joint ownership**, consisting of inherited or other property (**Article 851**) [1]. Such joint ownership is limited to a maximum period of **fifteen years**, with provisions for early withdrawal under court authorization or after six months' notice where no period is fixed (**Article 852**) [1]. Family joint ownership is governed by the rules relating to **joint property** and **mandate** (**Article 855**) [1].

---

## 10. Conflict of Laws and Public Policy

The Code contains a comprehensive conflict-of-laws framework: the **status and legal capacity** of persons are governed by the law of their nationality (**Article 11**) [1]. Foreign law will not be applied if its provisions are **contrary to Egyptian public policy or morality** (**Article 28**) [1]. These rules apply unless a **special law or international convention** provides otherwise (**Article 23**) [1].

---
